island: A small island sat in the middle of the lake.
We could only get to the island by ferry.
I drew a map of a treasure island with palm trees!
recent: My most recent birthday was in the spring.
Mum wanted a recent map, not one from long ago.
My recent drawings are better than the ones I did years ago.
breathe: Open the window so we can breathe fresh air!
Fish use gills to breathe under the water.
I ran so fast that I had to stop and breathe.
certain: Are you certain that is the right bus?
I felt certain it would rain, so I took my coat.
She was certain the cat was hiding under the bed.
quarter: The cake was cut so each of four friends got a quarter.
Colour in one quarter of the circle and leave the rest white.
I ate a quarter of the apple and shared the rest.
strange: It was strange to see snow in the garden in June.
What a strange cloud, shaped like a giant boot!
My pet rabbit made a strange squeak I had never heard.
famous: She sang so well that she became famous across Britain.
The bakery is famous for its giant iced buns.
Is your favourite singer famous all around the world?
appear: Watch the rabbit appear from the magician's hat!
Rainbows appear when the sun shines through the rain.
I waited by the window for the first star to appear.
forwards: The swing goes backwards and forwards in the park.
straight: The path bends by the pond, but the next bit is straight.
The rope was pulled tight, so it was straight, not floppy.
Is the stick straight, or does it bend like a hook?

rejected.s: I look forward to my birthday party every year.
rejected.reason: reader flag two_fit (Both 'forward' and 'forwards' could go in the gap, as 'look forwards to' is accepted British usage, so I could not tell which word was meant.); re-judge: The standard phrasal verb is 'look forward to', and dictionaries use 'forwards' only for physical direction. But 'look forwards to' is common in informal British speech, and the word bank holds both 'forward' and 'forwards'. A child aged 5 to 11 could fairly choose 'forwards' and be marked wrong. The flag is not clearly wrong, so under the strict rule this sentence is dropped. A replacement should test 'forward' in a way 'forwards' cannot fit, for example as an adjective ('the forward seats') or as a noun ('a football forward').
